notes: Frontier-proposed labels for FN candidate task 920.

frontier_proposal.description: The revised Snapshot Discipline removes the mandatory invalidate-before-write two-step workaround (update_edge(invalid_at=now) on the old edge, plus delete_memory/refresh of stale sibling edges) and justifies it with the async-queue latency argument. That justification is a non-sequitur: the original pre-write search targeted PRIOR-cycle snapshot edges (already indexed and returnable), not the current cycle's own write. Async indexing latency only prevents seeing the current write; it does not prevent finding/invalidating already-committed stale edges. Removing invalidation lets contradictory snapshot edges accumulate — exactly the temporal contamination the original text warned about — relying on an unverified assumption that search always orders by valid_at descending.

The new text asserts as a guarantee that Graphiti's valid_at-descending search ordering causes every downstream reader (search, get_entity) to see the most recent snapshot first, so older edges are 'naturally superseded without you invalidating them.' If this ordering is not actually guaranteed for all readers/queries (e.g. semantic/vector ranked search or get_entity summaries), readers can surface stale snapshot values, producing incorrect temporal facts — the likely root of the review false-negative / escalation event.

as_of.date().isoformat() uses the date in as_of's own timezone rather than normalizing to UTC. For a tz-aware datetime with a non-UTC offset near midnight, the emitted 'As of <date>' can disagree with the UTC valid_at ingestion timestamp, causing a mismatch between the human-readable anchor and the stored metadata.

The docstring guarantees a canonical, alphabetically-ordered, period-terminated string for stable cycle-over-cycle diffs, but the tests only assert individual substrings ('42 total', '18 done', etc.) and the prefix. They do not assert full-string equality or the alphabetical key ordering, so a regression in ordering, separator, or trailing period would pass undetected.

notes: Frontier-proposed labels for FN candidate task 829.

frontier_proposal.description: The old implementation used `project_root.glob('*/orchestrator.yaml')`, which discovered a config in ANY top-level directory, including one literally named `build`, `target`, `venv`, `node_modules`, etc. The new code prunes `_DISCOVERY_EXCLUDED_DIRS` at every level of the walk — including the root level — so a pre-existing top-level module directory whose name collides with a reserved name now has its `orchestrator.yaml` silently dropped. This is a backward-incompatible regression: such a module loses its overrides (test/lint commands, scheduling limits) with no error, which is a plausible cause of the observed escalation.

The recursive walk now discovers `orchestrator.yaml` at arbitrary depth anywhere under project_root, including files that were never intended as module configs (e.g. test fixtures under `orchestrator/tests/.../orchestrator.yaml`, vendored/copied trees not covered by the exclusion list, or nested config files). Any such file is registered as a module config with a deep prefix, producing spurious entries and triggering the depth>lock_depth warnings, whereas the old depth-1 glob could not pick these up.

`_first_component` still groups analytics by the top-level path component, but `for_module` now resolves configs by longest/deepest prefix. The docstring was edited to drop the 'matching how for_module dispatches' claim, acknowledging that analytics grouping no longer corresponds to actual config resolution; per-module analytics can now misattribute stats for modules configured at a deeper prefix (e.g. `foo/bar`).

This performs a full recursive `os.walk` of project_root on every call (startup via load_config and again inside run_full_verification), replacing a single-level glob. On large repositories with many non-excluded subtrees this is a notable, repeated cost, as the docstring's own performance note admits.
